sentences.text: Stegosaurus is an extinct herbivorous dinosaur easily recognized by a double row of vertical kite-shaped plates on its back and two pairs of horizontal spikes at the tail's end.
The animal possessed a long, narrow skull that was small relative to its massive body size.
While early collections from Carnegie included only a few postcranial remains, later crews eventually found dozens of specimens at Dinosaur National Monument.

Evidence of combat includes a punctured Allosaurus tail vertebra that fits perfectly with a Stegosaurus tail spike, and another Allosaurus specimen was killed when a Stegosaurus tail spike impaled its pubis, leading to a fatal infection.
A Stegosaurus skeleton remained on display at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science until 1989, when an expedition was sent to find additional remains for a hall revision.
The genus Stegosaurus was first described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1877 after he identified remains during the Bone Wars at Dinosaur Ridge.
The first fossils were actually discovered by Arthur Lakes and H.C. Beckwith north of Morrison, Colorado, at YPM Quarry 5.
Scientists generally agree that Stegosaurus used its spiked tails for defense and its plates primarily for display and secondarily for thermoregulation.
Stegosaurus sulcatus preserves a large spike, possibly from the shoulder, that is a key diagnostic feature of the species.

The hypothesis that Stegosaurus could rear up on its hind legs was proposed by Bakker and opposed by Carpenter, while a 2010 study by Mallison found support for a rearing posture in the related stegosaur Kentrosaurus, but not for its tail acting as a tripod.
A 2009 study found that Stegosaurus plates and spikes grew more slowly than the rest of the skeleton until the animal reached maturity.
A 2022 study suggests Stegosaurus likely had an ectothermic or gigantothermic metabolism similar to modern reptiles.

The sacro-lumbar expansion found in Stegosaurus also occurs in other ornithischians and in birds; in birds it contains a glycogen body, a structure postulated to supply glycogen to the nervous system.
Senter (2026) presents evidence of a limited range of motion for the fingers of Stegosaurus.
The type species of the genus Stegosaurus is Stegosaurus stenops.
Stegosaurus often falls within the subclade Stegosaurinae, which typically includes Wuerhosaurus and Hesperosaurus.
The International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature replaced the original type species with Stegosaurus stenops because the original type specimen was considered dubious.
Stegosaurus lived during the Late Jurassic period, specifically from the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian stages.
Stegosaurus fossils have been found in the western United States and Portugal, dating from 155 to 145 million years ago.
Stegosaurus lived alongside Apatosaurus, Diplodocus, Camarasaurus, and Allosaurus, the last of which may have preyed on it.
A 2019 study suggests that the sister group to Stegosauria, Ankylosauria, may have originated in the early Early Jurassic based on fossil evidence from India.
Four different arrangements of the plates have been proposed over the years, and Frederic Lucas eventually concluded that they were set in staggered rows.
